summary: This document defines a methodology for auditing Docusaurus blog articles to ensure readers see value quickly. It establishes three mechanical or qualitative passes that measure time-to-value (how far down the article before a reader sees a result), repetition (whether content is restated unnecessarily), and whether the opening 40 lines would make a stranger want to keep reading. The result is a single verdict — OK, MINOR, or RESTRUCTURE — that determines whether to file a TODO for fixes.

explanations.9: This skill is a set of rules and definitions, not the actual tool that runs audits; the /reader_review command is the tool that coordinates the workflow.
explanations.13: You should also load another reference document called 'blog-post-structure' that shows what the ideal article layout looks like, so you know what direction to point toward if restructuring is needed.
explanations.15: While examining code blocks, watch for values like port numbers or container names that appear in multiple commands — they should be declared once in a <Vars> component instead of hardcoded repeatedly.
explanations.27: The '<!-- truncate -->' marker is a Docusaurus convention that splits the preview readers see on the blog homepage from the full article they open; everything after it is the 'body' we're measuring.
explanations.39: T and E are variables: T is the line number where truncate appears, E is the total line count, and BODY is how many lines of content the reader faces after truncate.
explanations.42: If there is a <QuickJump> navigation component right after the truncate marker, move the truncate marker below it before measuring, because navigation scaffolding is not part of the actual content.
explanations.52: We only look at line numbers and positions, not read the whole article, so an audit of many articles stays fast and cheap to run.
explanations.54: Proof means the first moment the reader actually sees a working result, like command output or a screenshot.
explanations.62: If a <Terminal> tag references an external file, it will be short enough to skim; actually read it to confirm it is output, not just an install command.
explanations.64: If the article never shows any result anywhere, the TTV is 100% (the reader has to read the entire body before seeing any proof), and you should state this explicitly in your report.
explanations.87: This awk command counts the number of words in each section (between the ## headings) so you can see which sections are bloated.
explanations.105: When evaluating repetition, focus on whether facts are restated, not on making the article shorter; a long section that teaches new things is not a problem.
explanations.111: For the 30-second test, ignore everything except the title, description, and the first 40 lines after truncate — pretend you are a reader who knows nothing about this tool.
explanations.119: The pass 1 and pass 2 numbers (TTV percentage, redundancy count) are there to make audits consistent from article to article, but your gut reaction in the 30-second test is the real decision-maker.
explanations.132: MINOR findings do not generate TODOs because a batch of 40+ articles would have dozens of small one-line TODOs that drown out the real structural problems.
explanations.136: When you file a TODO to restructure, always frame it as moving existing blocks around, not cutting content, so the author knows nothing is being thrown away.
